hints: Notice how a plucked guitar string moves - it is pulled to one side and released, so its displacement is perpendicular to the length of the string.
Recall that transverse means oscillations perpendicular to energy travel and longitudinal means oscillations parallel to energy travel.
Think about what sound in air is - vibrating string pushes air back and forth to make compressions and rarefactions along the direction the sound travels.
walkthrough: Look at the plucked string: it is displaced sideways then released, so each part of the string oscillates at right angles to the string and to the direction the wave travels along the string.
By definition, oscillation perpendicular to wave travel is a transverse wave, so the wave on the string is transverse.
The vibrating string and guitar body push the surrounding air back and forth, creating regions of high and low air pressure.
In air, these compressions and rarefactions oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction the sound energy travels, which is the definition of a longitudinal wave.
So a transverse wave on the string causes a longitudinal sound wave in the air. This is option C.

options.A: The string does not vibrate with longitudinal waves when plucked sideways, so the first part is wrong even though sound in air is longitudinal.
options.B: Both parts are wrong because the plucked string vibrates transversely and sound in air cannot be transverse.
options.C: The plucked string vibrates perpendicular to its length so it is transverse, and its vibration produces compressions and rarefactions in air which are longitudinal sound waves.
options.D: The string wave is transverse but sound in air is not transverse, so the second part is wrong.
